Achievements & spotlights
The most credited
Jason Shirley leads with ten games, publisher staff on every one from Halo 2 through Halo Infinite. Six more follow at nine. Frank O'Connor spans 2004 to 2021, Community Team on Halo 2 and Franchise Creative Director on Halo Infinite, with no credit at all on Campaign Evolved. Greg Hermann holds a different title on nearly every game, from Engineering Lead on Halo 3: ODST through GM Game Director on Campaign Evolved, and Special Thanks only on Halo 5. Jimmy Bischoff, Joseph Staten, Pete Stacker and Phil Spencer round out the nine. Steve Downes and Jen Taylor, the voices of Master Chief and Cortana, sit close behind at eight.
Five who came back after 25 years
Adam Crockett, Mike Madeoy, Chris Wicklund, Mark Dias and Tawnya Pettiford-Wates share the longest gap on this sheet. All five worked on Combat Evolved in 2001 and return in Campaign Evolved in 2026, with nothing credited between. Adam is the odd one out: a Cinematic Artist turned Gameplay Animator, where the other four are voice actors reprising their roles. Three keep the same part: Private Bisenti, Private Mendoza, and Captain Carol "Foehammer" Rawley, the Pelican pilot Echo 419. Chris Wicklund plays PFC Fitzgerald. The 2001 credits also list him as Pvt. Jenkins, but Jenkins has no voice lines in the game, so Fitzgerald is the part he actually played.
The work moved outside
Combat Evolved credits no external studio at all. Halo Infinite credits 90 and Campaign Evolved 33, out of 226 across the franchise. Six in ten of the 9,174 people credited hold at least one vendor credit, so most of the people who built Halo were never employed by the studio named on the box. Campaign Evolved shows this most clearly. Virtuos fields 569 people across five of its studios, against a Halo Studios core team of 234.
Crossing the handoffs
92 people credited on Halo: Reach are credited again on Halo 4, spanning the handoff from Bungie to 343 Industries. 344 credited on Halo Infinite are credited again on Campaign Evolved, spanning the handoff from 343 Industries to Halo Studios. A credit on both sides of a handoff is not proof someone stayed on staff the whole way between them, only that their name was printed on both. Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori are the clearest case: credited on every game from Combat Evolved through Halo 4, then Special Thanks only on Halo 5 with no work credit, then credited again on most games after that for the original Bungie-era music being reused, not for anything new.
Improving MCC
872 people are credited in a Master Chief Collection release from 2018 onward who were not credited in the 2014 release, not counting anyone whose only appearance there is a reprint of an earlier game's roster. Two more games joined the collection, Halo 3 gained maps it never shipped with, and content kept arriving for years alongside the fixes. This is roughly how many extra hands all of that took.
Jeff Steitzer
The announcer on every game that shipped with multiplayer or Firefight. He has no real credit on Halo 2 or on either TMCC release, even though he recorded new lines for Halo 2: Anniversary multiplayer as part of TMCC. The gold dots on both TMCC releases are only his Combat Evolved credit carried forward as a reprint, not a new one.
External studios per game
Every studio credited on each game, with the number of people credited under it. Eighteen studios carry their own color, either because they recur across games or because they brought a large crew to one. Every other chip takes its border color from the kind of work it did: development, testing, cinematic and sound, or publishing. Hover a chip to see the label. A dashed chip marked ∅ means the credits name a company but list nobody under it, as Halo 2 does with "ReelFX Creative Studios, Inc. - Additional Cinematic Animation". The company was credited, so the chip carries no number.

  • Treat these numbers as a guide rather than a record. They are read from published credit rolls by software, and credit rolls misspell names, omit people, and credit the same person twice. Some mistakes will have survived that. The dataset is here for insight into how the work was staffed, and it should not be used to settle who did what.
  • Halo Wars, Halo Wars 2, Halo: Spartan Assault, Halo: Spartan Strike and Halo: Fireteam Raven are out of scope. This project covers the twelve mainline campaign releases; the strategy and arcade spin-offs are a different dataset.
  • Credits come from each game's first release, so the Halo PC and Halo 2 Vista ports are left out and their teams are not counted. MCC is the exception, because 343 Industries published separate credit rolls for its later updates. Those rolls name their own people, so they are counted separately. The two ports may be represented anyway, without being named: Halo CEA was built on the Halo PC port, MCC was built on Halo CEA, and MCC took its Halo 2 from the Vista port. Some of the people credited under Halo CEA or TMCC (2014) may therefore have earned that credit on the earlier port work. The credits do not say, and this is not confirmed.
  • A remaster or collection does not inherit the original's credits as a new one. Combat Evolved Anniversary, both Master Chief Collection releases, and Campaign Evolved all reprint earlier rosters rather than re-crediting them: Combat Evolved's roll carries into all four; Combat Evolved Anniversary's own roll carries into both Master Chief Collection releases too, since MCC's own 'Combat Evolved' runs on Anniversary's remade assets rather than the 2001 original; Halo 2, Halo 3 and Halo 4's carry into both Master Chief Collection releases as well; Halo 3: ODST and Halo: Reach's carry into the 2018 one only; and TMCC (2014)'s own roll -- credit for the compilation itself, not any one game in it -- carries into the 2018 release too, since that one is an update to the same compilation rather than a new one. A name that appears only in a reprint keeps its original credit and gains no new one, but does get a small gold marker on the poster wherever the reprint sits, so the connection is still visible -- a dot for anyone credited elsewhere too, since their row already has room for it, or a badge on their one chip for someone credited on nothing else, since giving all of them a dot of their own would have meant giving each their own row. Either marker means the same thing: a reprint, not a fresh credit. It draws no line to anything, and a real credit that comes later still counts as a gap after it.
  • Publisher staff and community volunteers are both counted, and neither counts toward any developer or vendor figure, since both sat outside the team that built the game. On the grid neither carries a marker of its own any more: 'publisher staff' and 'community volunteers' are role classes like any other now, coloured and keyed the same way engineering or art are. Each game's card still gives them their own segment in the 'by employer' bar, since that bar reads the roster by who staffed people rather than by what they did. MCC's February 2025 update is entirely community: 50 Reclaimer volunteers, credited alongside no developers at all.
  • Vendor share is hard to compare across eras. Bungie-era credits carry almost no vendor tags while 343-era credits are full of them. Part of that is real growth in outsourcing and part of it is a change in how credits were written.
  • Voice actors credited for localized versions are left out. Only the original English cast is counted, so a game dubbed into ten languages does not read as having ten times the cast.
  • Role categories are a best guess and will not all be right. Where a credit names someone's job, that is what is used. Where it does not, the role is read from the heading the credit sat under, from a department printed beside the name, or from the same person's entry on MobyGames.
Source: Halopedia, Halo Waypoint, IGDB and MobyGames credit rolls. Official cover art, promotional art, game logos and studio logos courtesy of Bungie, Xbox Game Studios, 343 Industries, Halo Studios and the various artists who made them.
